name: The Foucault Pendulum
statement: A freely swinging pendulum slowly turns its plane of swing, visibly proving the Earth rotates beneath it.
statementAccent: visibly proving the Earth rotates beneath it
meaning: The Foucault pendulum is a tall, freely swinging pendulum devised by the French physicist Léon Foucault and first demonstrated in 1851 in Paris, which provides a simple, direct demonstration that the Earth rotates. Foucault first showed it in the Meridian Room of the Paris Observatory in February 1851 and soon after mounted a famous large version under the dome of the Panthéon. The key observation is that, as the pendulum swings back and forth, the plane of its swing appears to rotate slowly relative to the floor beneath it over the course of hours. The pendulum itself tends to keep swinging in a fixed direction relative to space, while the Earth turns underneath it, so the apparent rotation of the swing plane is really the rotation of the ground, and hence of the Earth. The rate of this apparent rotation depends on latitude: at the poles the plane would make a full turn in one day, at the equator it would not rotate at all, and in between the rate is proportional to the sine of the latitude. The Foucault pendulum was the first straightforward laboratory demonstration of the Earth's rotation that did not depend on astronomical observation, and it remains a popular exhibit in science museums.
mechanism: A Foucault pendulum works because a long, heavy pendulum on a nearly frictionless, freely rotating suspension keeps swinging in a plane that is essentially fixed relative to the distant stars, that is, relative to an inertial frame of reference, while the Earth rotates beneath it. To an observer standing on the ground, who is turning with the Earth, the plane of the swing appears to rotate slowly in the opposite sense. In the rotating frame of the Earth, this apparent turning is attributed to the Coriolis force, the deflecting fictitious force that acts on moving objects in a rotating frame; the two descriptions, a fixed plane with a rotating Earth or a Coriolis deflection, are the same physics seen from different frames. The rate of the apparent rotation is not the same everywhere: it equals the Earth's rotation rate multiplied by the sine of the latitude, so it is a full three hundred sixty degrees per sidereal day at the poles and zero at the equator. At the latitude of Paris, about forty-nine degrees north, the swing plane precesses roughly eleven degrees per hour and completes a full circle in about thirty-two hours. A long wire and a heavy, symmetric bob keep the pendulum swinging steadily for hours so the slow rotation can be seen.

examples.text: Foucault's famous 1851 demonstration hung a heavy bob on a long wire under the dome of the Panthéon in Paris.
The swing plane turns a full circle per day at the poles, not at all at the equator, and at a rate set by the sine of the latitude between.
At the latitude of Paris the plane of swing precesses about eleven degrees an hour, completing a full turn in roughly thirty-two hours.

variants.name: The inertial-frame view
variants.text: The description in which the swing plane stays fixed relative to the stars while the Earth rotates beneath the pendulum.

whyItMatters: The Foucault pendulum is historically important as the first simple, direct, and public demonstration that the Earth rotates, requiring no telescope or astronomical measurement but only a long pendulum that anyone could watch. Before it, the Earth's rotation was inferred from the motions of the heavens; Foucault's pendulum made the rotation visible in a laboratory or a public hall, turning an abstract astronomical fact into something one could see with the eye over an afternoon. It vividly illustrates the physics of rotating reference frames and the Coriolis force, the same force that shapes weather systems and ocean currents, and it connects the everyday experience of a swinging weight to the grand fact of a spinning planet. Its dependence on latitude, with the swing plane turning fastest at the poles and not at all at the equator, is a beautiful and testable consequence of the geometry of rotation. Foucault pendulums remain among the most popular and instructive exhibits in science museums around the world.

limits: The Foucault pendulum demonstrates the Earth's rotation robustly, but its behavior depends on careful conditions. The apparent rotation rate varies with latitude as the sine of the latitude, so the plane turns fastest at the poles and not at all at the equator, and the roughly thirty-two-hour period is specific to the latitude of Paris rather than universal. A real pendulum must be long, heavy, and swing with very low friction and no sideways push at release, since imperfections in the suspension or an elliptical swing can introduce a spurious precession that masks or mimics the true effect, which is why demonstration pendulums are engineered carefully. The precise date of the Panthéon debut is given variously in sources, so it is best placed simply in 1851. The effect is equally well described as a fixed swing plane with a rotating Earth or as a Coriolis deflection in the rotating frame.
misreadings: The Foucault pendulum does not turn at the same rate everywhere; its apparent rotation depends on latitude, being fastest at the poles and absent at the equator. The roughly thirty-two-hour period is particular to Paris, not a universal figure. And the pendulum is not literally pushed around by the Earth touching it, but swings in a plane fixed relative to space while the Earth rotates beneath, equivalently a Coriolis effect, so treating the rotation as uniform everywhere, the Paris period as universal, or the effect as the Earth dragging the pendulum, misreads a latitude-dependent demonstration of the Earth's rotation.
origin: A pendulum devised by the French physicist Léon Foucault and first demonstrated in 1851 in Paris, the first simple laboratory demonstration of the Earth's rotation, its swing plane turning at a rate set by latitude.
